title: Workspace orchestration — cudaMalloc latency case notes
content:
Executive summary:

We observed a class of p99 latency spikes and occasional OOMs on multi-tenant Dedicated pools during mixed short/long prompt workloads. Unlike previous fragmentation incidents that correlated with long-lived KV cache growth, these incidents show high cudaMalloc latency bursts (10–200ms) that coincide with transient workspace pressure and rapid small-allocation patterns from concurrent streams.

This note documents the investigation steps, traces collected, experimental reproductions, and recommended mitigations. It focuses on the interaction between our workspace orchestration heuristics, cudaMalloc/cudaFree async behavior, and the host-side allocator fallbacks that surface as blocking cudaMalloc stalls.

1) Symptoms and context
- Service: text-generation-v2 model routes on Dedicated GPU pool (A100-40GB).
- Observable: 99.9th token latency spikes up to 450ms (baseline p99 ~65ms).
- Side effect: transient OOMs on a subset of workers during high burst traffic in the 02:00–03:00 PST window.
- Workload: bursty short-chat completions (seq_len 64) interleaved with long-batched requests (seq_len 2048) from one noisy tenant.
- Recent changes: workspace-orchestration rollout v1.4 (introduces aggressive evict-on-pressure heuristic).

2) Initial telemetry and trace artifacts
- nsys traces collected across 6 worker hosts (trace ids in linked_artifacts).
- Allocator logs enabled (RUNTIME_ALLOC_LOG=1) showed patterns: many small device allocations (~4–32KB) interleaved with large workspace grows (~100–500MB).
- NVTX markers show: allocation request -> stall -> large memcpy start. The stall aligns with cudaMalloc calls that fall back to synchronous driver allocation.
- Telemetry highlights: pct of cudaMalloc calls with >5ms latency rose from ~0.3% to ~4.7% during incident windows.

3) Reproduction plan and quick repro
- Repro harness: synthetic mixer that alternates: 8 short requests (seq64) per second and 1 long request (seq2048) every 3s, with 4 concurrent sessions.
- Repro results: reproduced p99 spikes and intermittent OOM on local staging with same GPU type when workspace-orchestration enabled. Disabling orchestration prevents the spikes (workspace kept pinned at conservative size).

4) Deep dive: allocator/driver interaction hypothesis
- Observation: Our allocator (slab/mempool) tries to avoid large synchronous cudaMalloc by reserving workspace slabs, but orchestration aggressively evicts slabs to free memory for other tenants.
- When eviction occurs, the runtime issues cudaMalloc to satisfy the next workspace grow. On A100 with persistence allocator behavior, this path can synchronize with driver housekeeping (page migrations, coherency) and block the calling thread for tens to hundreds of ms.
- Concurrent small allocations from inference kernels (per-stream scratch buffers) increase allocator fragmentation; freed small holes are not always coalesced quickly, forcing cudaMalloc to request new device memory rather than reuse.

5) Evidence snippets (abridged logs)
[2024-11-02T02:14:03.912Z] worker-7 INFO alloc: request workspace growth +320MB -> trying slab-reserve
[2024-11-02T02:14:03.922Z] worker-7 WARN evict: forcibly freed 480MB in eviction pass (candidate tenants: 3)
[2024-11-02T02:14:03.993Z] worker-7 DEBUG cudamalloc: start size=327680000
[2024-11-02T02:14:04.210Z] worker-7 DEBUG cudamalloc: end duration=217ms -> success
[2024-11-02T02:14:04.215Z] worker-7 INFO kernel: resumed dispatch (latency delta accounted)

6) Experiments attempted and outcomes
- Experiment A: Disable eviction-on-pressure for workspace-orchestration. Outcome: p99 spikes disappeared in repro. Memory usage increased modestly but stayed within pool limits.
- Experiment B: Increase small-allocation freelist coalescence timer (from 100ms -> 500ms). Outcome: reduced small-allocation misses by ~35%, fewer cudaMalloc fallbacks, p99 dropped ~18%.
- Experiment C: Switch to cuMemCreate/cuMemMap (CUDA MPS style) — prototype only. Outcome: eliminated blocking cudaMalloc but introduced complexity with host mapping and increased startup cost. Not production-ready.
- Experiment D: Force eager pre-allocation of per-request scratch pads (fixed-size per-session) instead of on-demand. Outcome: reduced churn but increased baseline reserved memory; OOMs avoided at cost of capacity loss.

7) Root-cause synthesis
- Primary driver: aggressive eviction combined with fragmented freelists leads to increased synchronous cudaMalloc calls that block worker threads while the driver performs device-side housekeeping (page migration / remapping).
- Secondary factors: workload mix (interleaved long/short requests) creates sudden large workspace needs that trigger eviction; many tiny allocations from kernels exacerbate fragmentation and freelist misses.

8) Short-term mitigations (low-risk ops changes)
- Roll back v1.4 eviction aggressiveness: revert to conservative grace window (500ms) before eviction. (Action: PR #893 in linked_artifacts)
- Increase freelist coalescence and add faster background coalescer thread to merge small holes when GPU idle.
- Add a temporary rate limiter that prevents >2 concurrent long-workspace grows per worker.
- Instrument a metric: cudaMalloc-block-duration histogram (labels: worker_id, tenant_id, request_id) to alert on growing tail.

9) Medium-term engineering work
- Improve allocator heuristics to prefer internal compaction over immediate cudaMalloc: attempt to relocate/migrate less-used tensors to host-pinned staging area before evicting slabs.
- Implement per-stream scratch pre-allocation with adaptive sizing (learned from traffic patterns) to reduce small-allocation churn.
- Explore adoption of CUDA virtual memory APIs (cuMem*): long-term, but requires host-side VMA and more complex lifecycle management. Prototype showed promise in eliminating blocking cudaMallocs, but needs safety and perf validation.

10) Monitoring and runbook updates
- Runbook: on alert of cudaMalloc-block-duration >50ms sustained for 5 minutes, triage steps: check eviction counts, recent orchestration config, noisy-tenant metrics, and consider temporary rollback of orchestration policy.
- Dashboard panels to add: per-worker allocation latency heatmap, freelist fragmentation ratio (free_chunks_count / total_chunks), eviction vs malloc-fallback timeline overlay.

11) Open questions & follow-ups
- Is there a correlation between CUDA driver version and observed blocking behavior for our GPU fleet? Need A/B across driver versions (work item).
- Can we build a fast simulated allocator model to explore fragmentation trade-offs for mixed-sequence workloads? (scheduling research spike)
- Should Dedicated pools expose an option to trade memory-headroom for lower tail latency (customer-configurable workspace-reserve)?

12) Action items (owners)
- Aisha: push rollback PR for eviction policy and monitor (ETA: 24h).
- Diego: instrument cudaMalloc-block-duration metric and dashboards (ETA: 48h).
- Lina: prototype background coalescer and freelist tuning across canary hosts (ETA: 2w).
- Marcus: driver-version A/B test on two small clusters (ETA: 1w).

Appendix: quick commands used
- nsys: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=cpu --output=trace-worker7.nsys python repro_harness.py
- allocator logging: export RUNTIME_ALLOC_LOG=1; tail -f /var/log/runtime/alloc.log | grep cudamalloc
- small alloc histogram extraction: python tools/alloc-inspector.py --input=alloc.log --bucket=power2

Notes to self: this feels like the allocator is being pressured into the slow path by orchestration policy; there is a neat medium-term win in moving to per-stream prealloc + smarter compaction. Avoid heavy driver-level experiments during peak traffic without a rollback path.

-- end of note --
